questions.question: Distinguish between point and non point sources of aquatic pollution with suitable examples
questions.solution_html:
• ecosystems
  • Oil Pollution refers to the contamination of water bodies with crude
  • oil, petroleum products, or their derivatives , which spread over the
  • water surface and affect aquatic life.
  • Oil spills from ships and tankers – Accidental discharge during
  • transportation.
  • Industrial discharge – Wastewater from petroleum refineries and
  • petrochemical industries.
  • Urban runoff – Oil from roads, garages, and machinery washed into
  • rivers and seas.
  • Offshore drilling – Leakage from oil rigs and pipelines.
  • Impact on Aquatic Ecosystems
  • Physical coating – Oil forms a layer on water, blocking sunlight and
  • reducing photosynthesis in aquatic plants.
  • Toxicity to organisms – Components like PAHs are toxic to fish
  • invertebrates, and plankton.
  • Oxygen depletion – Microbial breakdown of oil consumes dissolved
  • oxygen, leading to hypoxia.
  • Disruption of food chains – Oil bioaccumulates, affecting predators
  • and causing long-term ecological imbalance.
  • Habitat destruction – Shorelines and wetlands get coated with oil
  • damaging breeding and feeding grounds.
  • Explain how chemical pollutants affect the quality of water and
  • aquatic life. Alteration of water chemistry – Chemicals like acids
  • alkalis, and salts change pH, hardness, and conductivity, making
  • water unsuitable for many aquatic organisms. Toxic effects – Heavy
  • metals (lead, mercury, cadmium) and pesticides are toxic, causing
  • disease, reproductive failure, or death in fish and other organisms.
  • Eutrophication – Excess nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus
  • from fertilizers promote algal blooms, which block sunlight and
  • reduce oxygen levels when algae decay. Bioaccumulation and
  • biomagnification – Persistent chemicals accumulate in aquatic
  • organisms, leading to higher concentrations in predators , including
  • humans. Disruption of ecosystems – Chemical pollution can
  • eliminate sensitive species, reduce biodiversity, and destabilize food
  • chains.
questions.source_exam: Official Model Question Paper (FYUGP 2024
questions.final_answer: chains.

  • Ineffective for all pollutants – It may not remove highly toxic
  • volatile, or persistent chemicals efficiently, such as some heavy
  • metals or synthetic organics.

questions.question: Explain how heavy metals enter aquatic ecosystem.
questions.solution_html:
• Industrial discharge – Effluents from mining, metal processing
  • battery manufacturing, and electroplating industries release metals
  • like lead, mercury, cadmium, and chromium into water bodies.
  • Agricultural runoff – Use of pesticides, fertilizers, and sewage sludge
  • containing metals contributes to contamination.
  • Urban runoff and sewage – Waste from households, plumbing, and
  • urban areas carries metals such as copper, zinc, and nickel into
  • rivers and lakes.
  • Atmospheric deposition – Metals from air pollution (e.g., from
  • burning coal or smelting) settle on water surfaces or are washed
  • down by rain.
  • Natural sources – Weathering of rocks and volcanic activity can
  • release small amounts of metals into aquatic environments.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: release small amounts of metals into aquatic environments.

questions.question: Explain anthropogenic and natural pollution
questions.solution_html:
• Industrial discharge – Effluents from mining, metal processing
  • battery manufacturing, and electroplating industries release metals
  • like lead, mercury, cadmium, and chromium into water bodies.
  • Agricultural runoff – Use of pesticides, fertilizers, and sewage sludge
  • containing metals contributes to contamination.
  • Urban runoff and sewage – Waste from households, plumbing, and
  • urban areas carries metals such as copper, zinc, and nickel into
  • rivers and lakes.
  • Atmospheric deposition – Metals from air pollution (e.g., from
  • burning coal or smelting) settle on water surfaces or are washed
  • down by rain.
  • Natural sources – Weathering of rocks and volcanic activity can
  • release small amounts of metals into aquatic environments.

questions.question: What are the control and preventive measures of oil pollution?
questions.solution_html:
• Proper handling and transport of oil – Ensuring safe loading
  • unloading, and storage to prevent spills from ships, pipelines, and
  • tankers.
  • Oil spill containment – Using booms, barriers, and skimmers to
  • contain and remove oil from water surfaces immediately after a
  • spill.
  • Use of dispersants and absorbents – Chemicals or materials that
  • break down or absorb oil, reducing its spread and impact.
  • Regular maintenance of equipment – Preventing leaks from
  • refineries, offshore rigs, and machinery through proper inspection
  • and repair.
  • Wastewater treatment – Treating industrial effluents containing oil
  • before discharging into water bodies.
  • Legislation and monitoring – Enforcing strict environmental
  • regulations and continuous monitoring to minimize accidental
  • discharges.
